title: README bump lands AFTER the tag, so every published tarball's npm page advertises the PREVIOUS version
description:
MEASURED 2026-09-15 against the registry, not inferred:

  npm view @opum-ai/lore@0.7.0 readme
    line 33: "Published on npm as **`@opum-ai/lore@0.6.2`**"
    line 39: "> **Status: 0.6.2 released.** Tag `v0.6.2` ..."

The npm landing page for the CURRENT release tells a user the current release is the
previous one. package.json `files` is ["bin","README.md","LICENSE"], so README.md is
shipped in the tarball and is what the registry serves as the package page.

CAUSE IS ORDERING, NOT FORGETFULNESS. The README current-state bump is authored as
post-release bookkeeping: v0.7.0 was tagged, then commit 2b6181df ("0.7.0 is released
-- replace the release-truth and README current-state claims", PR #99) landed on dev
afterwards. A doc that asserts "X is released" cannot honestly be written before X is
released, so the honest sentence and the shipped bytes are structurally in tension.
The tag therefore always carries the PRIOR version's README, and always will, for as
long as the claim is phrased in the past tense.

THIS IS A RECURRENCE, NOT A ONE-OFF. LCLI-325 is the same defect one minor line down:
"README Install section still pins 0.1.0 and describes the shipped 0.2.0 install fix
as a future release". It was fixed as an incident. The mechanism that produces it was
not, so it came back. Fix the mechanism.

WHY IT IS NOT COSMETIC. The install instructions and the status block are the first
thing a new user reads, and they currently disagree with the artifact they just
installed. It also undercuts the lockstep sentence: README line 42 on dev says "the
two version numbers move in lockstep", while npm currently shows lore 0.7.0 against
quest 0.7.1.

THE OBVIOUS FIX IS THE WRONG ONE. "Remember to bump the README before tagging" is a
runbook line, and the fleet rule is to prefer a fix that removes the need for
judgement. Two shapes that do:
  (a) Stop the README asserting a version at all -- point at the release-truth doc
      and at npm's own version badge, so there is nothing to go stale.
  (b) Derive the version-bearing lines from package.json at release time, and add a
      check that fails the release when the README's stated version is not the
      version being tagged.
(b) also catches the case where someone tags without touching the README at all.

SCOPE NOTE: this is a release-machinery defect, not a code defect. It is realised by
the NEXT publish. Landing it after a 0.7.1 is cut buys nothing.
implementationNotes:
THE MECHANISM IS UNFIXED IN TWO REPOSITORIES, NOT ONE. Measured by opum-agent 2026-09-15T17:40Z after re-verifying the lore half independently, then applying this record's own reasoning across a repository boundary:

  npm view @opum-ai/quest@0.7.1 readme  ->  'Published on npm as @opum-ai/quest@0.6.0' / 'Status: 0.6.0 released.'
  npm view @opum-ai/quest@0.7.0 readme  ->  identical

So quest has TWO published versions of a public package both advertising 0.6.0, where lore has one advertising 0.6.2. Same cause, same post-tag bookkeeping order, neither repository aware of the other's instance.

THIS UNDERSTATES WHAT I FILED ABOVE AND THE CORRECTION MATTERS. I framed this as LCLI-325 recurring because it was fixed as an incident rather than as a mechanism. The accurate framing is stronger: the mechanism was never fixed ANYWHERE, and its second host was found only because someone asked whether a defect shape respects repository boundaries. It does not. A per-repo fix here would leave quest's instance standing and would not be a fix of the mechanism at all.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE FIX, and it is a real constraint rather than a note: published version pages are IMMUTABLE. Neither 0.7.0's nor 0.7.1's npm page can be corrected retroactively. Whatever we build can only be PROVEN at the next publish, which means the proof is a release-time measurement and cannot be demonstrated in CI on a green tree. Design the check so it fails a release rather than so it passes a test.

OPEN AND NOT MINE TO SETTLE: whether lore and quest fix this as one coordinated mechanism or two parallel ones. opum-agent has suggested coordination to quest-cli and explicitly not directed it. Worth answering before either side writes code, because option (b) in the description -- derive the version and fail the release on disagreement -- is the kind of thing that wants to be one shared script rather than two that drift.

IMPLEMENTATION FINDING: A3 CLAUSE 3 AS LANDED WOULD CATCH ONE OF THIS README'S FOUR STALE SITES. Raised by quest-cli from its own implementation (QCLI PR #132), measured here against the published artifact.

Clause 3 scopes to "no occurrence of the package's own name adjacent to a version outside the region". Measured on lore@0.7.0's README -- the published one, which is the artifact the defect actually happened to:

  line 33   `@opum-ai/lore@0.6.2`                       HAS package name -> CAUGHT
  line 39   **Status: 0.6.2 released.** Tag `v0.6.2`     no package name -> MISSED
  line 41   ... agree on `0.6.2`                         no package name -> MISSED
  line 47   ...                                          no package name -> MISSED

FOUR sites, not the two that were previously recorded on this task. Clause 3 catches ONE, and the three it misses include LINE 39 -- the "Status: 0.6.2 released" claim that the entire contract was written around. The package name nearest to line 39 sits on line 40 ("all seven public `@opum-ai/lore*` npm packages"), so any same-line adjacency rule misses it, and any adjacency window wide enough to reach it is wide enough to be meaningless.

quest-cli's README has the identical structure -- its stale Status: is line 23 with the package name on line 24 -- so this is a property of how both projects write a status block, not a quirk of one.

WHY THIS DOES NOT INVALIDATE THE CONTRACT. Clauses 1 and 2 (region present, region byte-equal to generated) are unaffected and still do the primary work. Clause 3's job is only to constrain what lies OUTSIDE the region, and it turns out to do that job for one shape of stale site and not the common one. The contract is right that something must constrain the outside; the specific predicate is too narrow.

WHY quest-cli ESCAPED IT AND THIS REPOSITORY CANNOT. They took A2's ABSENT arm -- their README now states no version at all -- so they could strengthen clause 3 to "no version token anywhere outside the region", which is free when the file has zero tokens. This README has NINE legitimate non-package version tokens (Backlog.md >=1.49.0, Bun 1.3.14, historical 0.2.0 and 0.6.x). A no-token rule is unusable here for exactly the reason it is free there, so the scoped predicate is the only form available and it has to be a better predicate rather than a stronger one.

CANDIDATE PREDICATES, none chosen yet -- this is the decision the implementation has to make:
  (a) Region covers ALL FOUR sites rather than the Status: line alone. Reduces
      what clause 3 must catch, but does not remove the need for it.
  (b) Adjacency computed over the enclosing BLOCK (blockquote, list item,
      paragraph) rather than the line. Line 39 and line 40 are one blockquote,
      so this catches it without an arbitrary line window.
  (c) Forbid outside the region only versions matching THIS package's released
      or previously-released values -- a closed set read from the changelog or
      the registry -- so 1.49.0 and 1.3.14 are legal and 0.6.2 is not.

(b) is the most likely right answer and is testable: the proof must include a
Status:-style line whose package name is on the NEIGHBOURING line, which is
exactly the case a same-line matcher passes.

PROOF REQUIREMENT ADDED, from quest-cli's own run: prove against BOTH shapes
separately -- a package-name-adjacent site and a Status:-style site with the name
one line away -- because only the second distinguishes a working predicate from
clause 3 as written. Their four-run proof (clean 0, defect A 1, defect B 1,
restored 0) is the shape to copy.

CORRECTION TO THE NOTE ABOVE: THREE STALE SITES, NOT FOUR. And the distinction is not bookkeeping -- it eliminates one of the three candidate predicates.

opum-doc pushed back on the count and is right. The object I measured was "lines carrying the string 0.6.2". The object the claim needed was "lines ASSERTING a stale current version". Those differ by exactly one line:

  33  Published on npm as `@opum-ai/lore@0.6.2`          asserts 0.6.2 IS current  -> FALSE at 0.7.0
  39  **Status: 0.6.2 released.** Tag `v0.6.2`,          asserts 0.6.2 IS current  -> FALSE at 0.7.0
  41  and a clean-room registry install agree on `0.6.2` asserts 0.6.2 IS current  -> FALSE at 0.7.0
  47  `0.6.2` was therefore published with               narrates HOW 0.6.2 shipped
      `scripts/publish-release.sh` and, like                                       -> STILL TRUE at 0.7.0

Line 47 is a historical statement about a past release, true at 0.7.0 for the same reason `1.3.14` and `>=1.49.0` are true. It is not a stale site. It sits inside the stale block, so A2 removes it either way and THE REMEDY IS UNCHANGED -- but the predicate is not.

THIS KILLS CANDIDATE (c). A closed set of this package's own released values, forbidden outside the region, condemns line 47 -- and would condemn every honest historical citation of a past version, which this README has more of than most (0.2.0, 0.6.0, 0.6.1, 0.6.2 all appear legitimately somewhere). (c) is withdrawn.

(b), block-scoped adjacency, SURVIVES the caveat and is now the clear choice: lines 39 and 40 are one blockquote, so it catches 39 without a window wide enough to be meaningless, and it says nothing about whether line 47's claim is current -- which is correct, because that is not its job.

(a), widening the region, remains available and composes with (b) rather than competing.

THE ERROR IS THE SAME ONE THIS WHOLE THREAD IS ABOUT, and it is mine, and it is the sixth instance across three sessions. I counted the string rather than the claim, then wrote the count into a task, a PR body and two messages. What makes it worth recording rather than just fixing: the miscount was CONSERVATIVE-LOOKING -- four sounds worse than three, so it read as thorough rather than as wrong, and nobody checking my work for over-claiming would have flagged it. An error that exaggerates the problem you are fixing is not self-correcting; it is the one that recruits agreement.

PROOF REQUIREMENT, RESTATED with opum-doc's ranking. The two SHAPES matter more than the run count: a name-adjacent site, and a Status:-style site with the package name on the neighbouring line. A four-run proof that uses the same shape twice proves the gate RUNS, not that it CATCHES. This is the fleet rule about proving rejection and acceptance separately, with a second axis on it.

SESSION HANDOFF 2026-09-15. This is the ACTIVE thread. Read the two notes above this one before acting; they carry the measurements, not this one.

LIVE STATE AT HANDOFF, verified rather than remembered:
  branch  lcli-510-clause3-finding @ 06846897, clean, pushed
  PR      #117 OPEN against dev, CI in progress at handoff
  dev     fa4f6678

FIRST ACTION FOR THE SUCCESSOR: land PR #117. Verify the run whose headSha EQUALS
06846897 (or the tip if amended) -- `gh run list --branch <b> --json headSha,databaseId`
and match, because `gh run list --limit 1` returns the previous run and passes
instantly. Confirm all five required contexts by name, two of which carry U+00B7
not an ASCII period. Then `gh pr merge 117 --squash --delete-branch`; if that exits
non-zero, check `gh pr view 117 --json state` BEFORE re-running -- a dirty tracker
file blocks only the local post-merge branch switch and prints "Aborting" AFTER a
successful merge (found by opum-doc).

CORRECTION THE SUCCESSOR WILL LIKELY INHERIT WRONG. An orchestrator brief in
circulation says "each README has TWO stale sites, not one". Both numbers are
superseded. The measured answer for lore@0.7.0 is THREE:
  33  Published on npm as `@opum-ai/lore@0.6.2`   asserts current -> FALSE
  39  **Status: 0.6.2 released.** Tag `v0.6.2`,   asserts current -> FALSE
  41  ... registry install agree on `0.6.2`       asserts current -> FALSE
  47  `0.6.2` was therefore published with ...    narrates PAST   -> STILL TRUE
Line 47 is history and is NOT a stale site; I counted it as one and opum-doc
recounted. Do not restore "four", and do not accept "two".

WHAT IS DECIDED, so it is not re-opened:
  - Contract is ODOC-201, landed in opum-doc docs/reference/shipped-readme-version-
    assertions.md. main was 0af2525 at handoff; their PR #288 amends the clause-3
    rationale with the disjoint-coverage argument, so CITE THE AMENDED PARAGRAPH,
    not the first-landed one. They owe me that SHA.
  - Shape (b) of the contract: two implementations, one agreed text. quest-cli
    implemented in its PR #132.
  - lore takes A2's GENERATED arm; quest took the ABSENT arm. Consequence that
    matters for A5: quest's README now has zero version tokens, which kills A3's
    byte-equality clause there by construction, so LORE IS THE ONLY SIDE
    ENFORCING IT. The two implementations exercise disjoint parts of the
    contract; neither alone is evidence it works. Say that in lore's A5 line.

THE OPEN DECISION, and it is the next real work: A3 clause 3 as landed catches ONE
of the three stale sites. It scopes to "the package's own name adjacent to a
version", and line 39's nearest package name is line 40, inside the same
blockquote. Candidates:
  (a) widen the marked region to cover all three sites -- composes with (b)
  (b) compute adjacency over the enclosing BLOCK rather than the line -- PREFERRED
  (c) WITHDRAWN. A closed set of this package's own released values condemns
      line 47, which is honest history, and every other legitimate past-version
      citation. It reads tighter than (b) on paper and is wrong.

PROOF REQUIREMENT, non-negotiable and the reason this is written down: prove
against BOTH SHAPES separately -- a name-adjacent site, AND a Status:-style site
whose package name is on the neighbouring line. Only the second distinguishes a
working predicate from clause 3 as written. A four-run proof using the same shape
twice proves the gate RUNS, not that it CATCHES. Left to itself this session would
have proved against `@opum-ai/lore@0.6.2`, got a red, and shipped a check missing
two of three sites -- believing it, because it agreed with the expectation.

A MEASUREMENT THE SUCCESSOR MUST NOT REDO FROM MEMORY: lore's README on dev carries
NINE semver tokens that are not the package version (counting occurrences of a
semver token != package version), all legitimate -- Backlog.md >=1.49.0, Bun
1.3.14, historical 0.2.0/0.6.x. That is why quest's "no version token anywhere"
rule is free for them and unusable here.

PEERS: quest-cli (implementer, other half of A5) and opum-doc (owns ODOC-201).
Both are mid-thread and expect to hear what predicate lore picks BEFORE it is
implemented, because A5 only means something if each side knows what the other
enforces.

HANDOFF ADDENDUM: THE AMENDED CONTRACT SHA ARRIVED. The note above says opum-doc owes it; it does not any more.

  CITE:        opum-ai/opum-doc  main@0708fe5
  DOCUMENT:    docs/reference/shipped-readme-version-assertions.md
  DO NOT CITE: 0af2525 -- the first-landed version, missing the clause-3 work an
               implementer needs. ODOC-201 is Done.

WHAT 0708fe5 ADDS over the text this repository proposed, both from implementation
rather than drafting:
  1. A3 clause 3 is now stated as A FLOOR, NOT A SUFFICIENT CHECK. Confirmed
     against both published READMEs -- lore lines 33/39/41, quest 16/23/25 -- only
     the first of each is caught.
  2. The disjoint-necessity argument for keeping BOTH clause 3 and the marked
     region: a Status:-only region leaves the "Published on npm as" bullet stale
     and clause 3 catches it; a name-adjacency rule leaves the Status: line stale
     and only the region catches it. Neither covers the other's site.

A5 IS BEING AMENDED, tracked as ODOC-203, and the successor should read it before
writing lore's A5 line rather than writing the line twice. The amendment is the
point this repository raised and opum-agent sharpened from outside both repos:
lore took A2's GENERATED arm and quest took ABSENT, so quest's README will have
zero version tokens and A3's byte-equality clause is VACUOUS there by
construction. Lore is the only side that will ever exercise it. The consequence
ODOC-203 states is the one that matters: THE UNION OF IMPLEMENTATIONS IS THE UNIT
OF PROOF -- two green repositories read as corroboration when they are in fact
coverage, and a byte-equality defect would be invisible in quest and load-bearing
here.

STATE OF THE OTHER SIDE, measured by opum-doc against refs rather than working
trees: lore's README at origin/dev carries "Status: 0.7.0 released" and 15 semver
tokens; quest's still carries "Status: 0.6.0" and 4, because its zero-token fix is
on its PR #132 and NOT YET MERGED. So quest's side is not done, and a successor
checking quest's README today will find the defect still present. That is expected,
not a regression.

SESSION HANDOFF 2026-09-15, recycled for context. LCLI-510 is IMPLEMENTED and PUSHED but NOT
LANDED. Read this note before the older ones; they carry the measurements that led here, this
one carries live state and the single next action.

LIVE STATE, verified rather than remembered:
  branch  fix/LCLI-510-shipped-readme-version-gate @ 159f7d2d, clean, pushed
  PR      #118 OPEN against dev
  CI      run 35018449156 on 159f7d2d was IN FLIGHT at handoff -- 3 jobs left, none failed
  dev     fe1bdc95
  PROVEN GREEN: run 35017881343 on de319a1f, conclusion success, zero failed jobs,
  INCLUDING lint . typecheck . test (windows-latest). de319a1f is the parent of 159f7d2d,
  so everything except the N+1 region tests is already measured green on a real run.

FIRST ACTION FOR THE SUCCESSOR: resolve the run whose headSha EQUALS the tip
(gh run list --branch <b> --json headSha,databaseId and match -- gh run list --limit 1
returns the PREVIOUS run and passes instantly). Confirm all five required contexts BY NAME;
two carry U+00B7, not an ASCII period. Then close this task IN PR #118 (final summary +
quest complete, citing PR number and run id, never the merge SHA), and squash-merge.

WHEN GATING ON CI, gate on status == completed FIRST. An in-progress job returns conclusion
as an EMPTY STRING, not null: a jq filter of select(.conclusion != null and .conclusion !=
\"success\") reports every running job as failed. This session wrote that filter, briefly
believed seven jobs had failed, and only caught it because the count was implausible.

WHAT LANDED. The README's version lines are GENERATED from package.json, and the release
REFUSES to publish a tarball whose packed README disagrees.
  scripts/shipped-readme-version.mjs  --write generates, --check reads the worktree,
                                      --tarball IS the gate
  release.yml package job             gate, immediately after npm pack
  release.yml publish job             A4 read-back: re-runs --check over the bytes the
                                      REGISTRY served
  publish-release.sh                  the same tarball gate before any registry write
  ci.yml (via bun test)               --check on the real README every PR -- early
                                      feedback, explicitly NOT the gate
  docs/reference/shipped-readme-version-record.md   the A5 record, per clause

publish-release.sh is NOT redundant with the workflow: it publishes whatever is in its
artifacts dir, which its own usage text says an operator may populate by hand, and the root
launcher is simultaneously the ONLY package shipping a README and the only one with no
independently recorded qualification digest.

THE RUNBOOK LINE THAT CAUSED THIS IS GONE. publish-release.sh's closing message told the
operator to update README.md AFTER publishing while the runbook said to reconcile it with the
version bump. Two instructions disagreed and the post-publish one won every time. Step 1 no
longer lists README.md and says why, so nobody restores it.

THE PREDICATE, which was the open decision: (b) BLOCK-SCOPED adjacency. A block is a maximal
run of lines delimited by a blank line or a blockquote-internal '>'. Clause 3 fires when one
block holds both this package's own npm name and a version token, with every region's CONTENT
masked BYTE-WISE first. NOT quest's no-token-anywhere rule (free at zero tokens, nine false
positives here). NOT (c), a closed set of released values -- condemns honest history,
withdrawn. Two regions, boundaries set by what is GENERABLE: a spanning region would enclose
the '0.6.2 was therefore published' narration, which is not derivable from package.json, so
byte-equality would force the generator to FABRICATE history.

FOUR DEFECTS FOUND AFTER THE GATE WAS ALREADY GREEN. This is the part worth carrying forward,
because all four came from interrogating the artifact rather than re-reading the check:
1. RENDERING. Markers sat right after '- ' and '> ', so each line's CONTENT began with '<!--',
   which starts a CommonMark HTML block that emits the REST OF THAT LINE as raw text. GitHub's
   own POST /markdown showed the npm page rendering a literal '**Status: 0.7.0 released.**',
   asterisks and all -- while every version assertion passed. A correct gate, a green suite and
   a broken page simultaneously. Markers now anchor AFTER hand-written text.
2. A4 WOULD HAVE GONE RED ON A CORRECT RELEASE. It grepped for a literal the markers split. It
   now re-runs --check over the served bytes, so the assertion cannot drift from the generator
   because it IS the generator.
3. NO ESCAPE HATCH EXISTED for clause 3, so the first legitimate '@opum-ai/lore@<old>' in prose
   would have forced someone to widen the predicate. Added hand-written allow spans, masked for
   clause 3 only, never byte-checked, unterminated ones refused.
4. THE N+1th REGION was unproven. Regions are declared in CODE, and every other test exercised
   exactly the two that exist, so a machine specialised to them would have passed the whole
   suite. Tests now patch a COPY of the real script to declare a third region and run the real
   binary against three.

PROOF. lore 0.7.0, quest 0.7.1, Bun 1.3.14, Node 24.20.0, macOS. Acceptance and rejection as
SEPARATE measurements on real npm pack tarballs: clean 0.7.0 exit 0; a 0.7.1 tarball with the
README left as post-tag bookkeeping exit 1 with both regions named -- the defect itself.
Four clause-3 shapes, each labelled by the WRONG IMPLEMENTATION it passes under (one line /
name on the next line / two lines following a region / sharing a marker's line). Mutation
matrix, eight wrong implementations, unmutated 0 of 33. The row that matters is 'region
excision made line-wise -> 1' -- a one-test margin, which a pass total would hide.

WINDOWS. Both A1 tests failed on windows-latest and nowhere else (run 35016083790):
'tar (child): Cannot connect to C: resolve failed'. GNU tar reads C:\\... as a host:path remote
spec; --force-local fixes GNU tar and does NOT exist in the bsdtar macOS ships. Script and
tests now run tar from the file's own directory with a bare filename. Production never reaches
that path, so a required context exercised a path the release never takes and found a real
script defect anyway. Reported to opum-agent as a fleet-level observation.

CONTRACT: opum-doc docs/reference/shipped-readme-version-assertions.md at main@ba3055d.
Superseded, do NOT cite: d56ea3f, b596ca5, 7af9f7d, 0708fe5, 0af2525. Four corrections this
implementation reported were landed into it.

A5: lore-cli is the ONLY side that will ever exercise A3 byte-equality -- quest took A2's
absent arm, so theirs is vacuous by construction. The record names the MUTATION MATRIX as its
evidence rather than a green CI run, because a green run is what would NOT distinguish it.

NOT DONE HERE, deliberately: README line 42's 'pair with quest 0.7.0' lockstep claim is
hand-maintained and outside both regions. It asserts ANOTHER package's version so it is out of
A2's scope; reconciling it is LCLI-511.

PEERS: quest-cli and opum-doc are both mid-thread and both expect ONE more message -- the
green head run id with per-job confirmation, so they can upgrade their A5 records from
'decided and locally measured' to proven. I sent quest-cli a run id while it was still
IN PROGRESS and it later failed; they caught it. Their framing, which is the better one:
AN IDENTIFIER LOOKS LIKE EVIDENCE -- a run id reads as more checked than a sentence while
carrying less, because a sentence at least announces itself as a claim. Do not repeat it.

SESSION CONTEXT-COST OBSERVATION, 2026-09-15, recorded at the orchestrator's request rather
than because it is a fact about LCLI-510. It is here because .claude/handovers/ is gitignored
so the cursor does not travel, which makes a tracker note the only durable place a process
observation survives a recycle.

ONE CORRECTION TO THE FRAMING FIRST, because the diagnosis depends on it. The brief said
'second recycle in about half an hour'. The restart cursor this session started from was
written 2026-09-15T19:06:11Z and this handoff is ~20:17Z, so the interval is ~70 minutes, not
~30. That matters: a 30-minute burn suggests something pathological, a 70-minute one spent
almost entirely inside a single implementation-plus-proof cycle suggests ordinary cost for
this KIND of task. Both readings call for different fixes, so the number is worth getting
right before acting on it.

WHAT ACTUALLY CONSUMED IT, ordered by my estimate of size, largest first:

1. THE HARNESS RE-DISPLAYING WHOLE FILES AFTER EVERY BASH EDIT. This is the big one and it is
   avoidable. I made most edits with `python3 - <<PY` heredocs rather than the Edit tool.
   Editing a file the session has already read via Bash triggers a
   '[This command modified N files you have previously read]' system-reminder that echoes the
   changed file back with line numbers -- repeatedly 100-150+ lines, and it fired on nearly
   every patch. Across ~20 such edits this was almost certainly the single largest consumer,
   and it bought nothing: I had just written the content.
   FIX, and it is mechanical: use the Edit tool for edits to files already in context. Edit
   does not re-dump. Reach for a heredoc only for genuinely bulk or generated rewrites, and
   accept the echo as the price when you do.

2. TRACKER READS THAT DUMP THE WHOLE RECORD. `quest task view LCLI-510 --plain` prints the
   full description AND every implementation note. LCLI-510 carries five long ones, so a
   single view is several thousand tokens, and I ran it more than once. `quest task list
   --status \"In Progress\" --plain` does the same thing for every matching task -- it printed
   this entire record again just to answer 'which task is In Progress'.
   FIX: for the id alone use `--json` with a jq projection, or `quest board`. Read the full
   record ONCE at session start and never again; the notes do not change under you.
   WORTH RAISING UPSTREAM: `quest task list` has no summary/oneline mode, so asking 'what is
   In Progress' costs the full text of every In Progress task. That is a real missing
   capability rather than a usage mistake.

3. CROSS-SESSION MESSAGES. Eight arrived, several 700-1000 words. They were high-value -- two
   of them changed the implementation -- so this is not waste, but it is a cost that scales
   with peer count and is invisible when planning. A three-way design conversation is
   expensive by construction.

4. SKILL LOADS. opum-sdlc, opum-handoff, and `lore instructions`. Each is a few thousand
   tokens. Unavoidable and correct, but worth knowing they are not free: loading opum-sdlc to
   confirm a branch-naming convention I already followed was probably not worth its price.

5. READING THE FULL CONTRACT DOCUMENT (302 lines) from opum-doc. Correct and load-bearing --
   I was implementing against it and a summary would have been a relayed measurement -- but it
   is a large single read.

6. CI POLLING, which is the one the brief named and which I believe is NOT a significant
   consumer here. Individual `gh run view --json` calls with jq projections are tens of tokens.
   The genuinely expensive CI read was ONE `gh run view --log-failed` piped through grep.
   Naming polling as a cost driver would have sent the next session optimising the cheapest
   thing on this list. I already moved the waiting itself to background until-loops, which is
   the right shape and costs one notification each.

THE STRUCTURAL POINT, which outlives the specific numbers: this task took four
implement-measure-correct cycles AFTER the first green gate, because each defect was found by
inspecting the artifact rather than by re-running the check. That is the correct way to build a
gate and it is inherently context-expensive -- every cycle re-reads files, re-runs suites and
